newsitem.title: India: Legal net tightens around former Indian PM Rao.
newsitem.headline: Legal net tightens around former Indian PM Rao.

text.p: An Indian court indicted former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao on Tuesday in a vote-buying case, dealing another legal setback to the embattled politician who quit in disgrace last year as Congress party leader.
But Judge Ajit Bharihoke rejected a request that Rao's successor, as leader of India's oldest party, Sitaram Kesri, be summoned in the same scandal.

The judge, presiding over a special court of inquiry, ruled there was sufficient evidence to try Rao for criminal conspiracy and abetment to bribery, the counsel for the former prime minister, R.K. Anand, told Reuters.
Both charges carry a maximum penalty of five years in prison if the accused is convicted, Anand said.
Rao is the first Indian prime minister or former prime minister to ever face criminal charges.
Bharihoke set May 14 for arraignment when Rao and 19 other accused in the four-year-old case will be asked to enter a plea. A trial would follow for those who plead not guilty.

The judge's decision on Tuesday was the latest blow to Rao, who led India for five years from 1991 and oversaw major cuts in trade and investment barriers before suffering a crushing defeat in general elections last year.

Rao has been named in two other criminal cases relating to forgery and cheating a businessman. He has denied wrongdoing in all of the cases and has obtained preventive bail in all three, which are before courts in New Delhi.
Rao quit as Congress chief last September after a judge ordered him to appear in court in the criminal cheating case.

Before Rao, no Indian prime minister or former prime minister had ever faced criminal charges. Former prime minister Indira Gandhi was summoned to court in 1975 to face civil charges in a case of election irregularities, but was never punished.

Anand said Rao was innocent in a case involving allegations that in 1993 he tried to influence a parliamentary vote of no-confidence by bribing four deputies of a tribespeople's party in the eastern state of Bihar. Rao's minority government defeated the no-confidence motion by a narrow margin.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is investigating payments of three million rupees ($84,000) into a bank account held by a member of the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM) party.
The CBI had already charged Rao and the others in the vote-buying case. The judge on Tuesday agreed that there was adequate evidence to proceed to trial, a CBI spokesman said.

Anand said Bharihoke rejected a legal request that the court summon the current Congress president, Sitaram Kesri, in the vote-buying case. Kesri had been accused by one of the JMM leaders who allegedly received a bribe.
Among the 19 others accused in the case were several former government ministers. All have denied involvement in the case.
Anand said he would file a petition asking the Delhi High Court to discharge the vote-buying charges against Rao.
"It still has to go to trial and there has been no conviction," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told Reuters. "We are confident he (Rao) has a good case. It can't harm Congress."
Voter surveys showed that a rash of scandals while Rao was in power contributed to his party's historic defeat last year.
But other major parties, including the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party and Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party, have also had to contend with corruption cases.

The CBI recently announced it would prosecute Janata Dal leader Laloo Prasad Yadav in a $280 million "animal fodder" scandal, marring Gujral's start in office. Yadav has said he is innocent, but party leaders are pressing him to step down. ($1= 35.8 rupees)
